title: Analytics Primer
text:
An guide to the quantitative models across WoSo.Live.
Soccer is a fluid, low-scoring game where traditional counting statistics - such as goals, assists, and clean sheets - routinely tell misleading stories.
A striker might score a hat trick of simple tap-ins created entirely by her teammates, while an elite playmaker creates five clear-cut openings that her forwards fail to convert. Similarly, a goalkeeper might earn a clean sheet without facing a single difficult shot, while another concedes three times after facing ten point-blank strikes.
The analytics models across WoSo.Live look past surface results to measure what actually occurred on the pitch, operating across four distinct layers:

title: Analytics Primer
text:
1. Expected Goals (xG): Evaluating Chance Creation
Expected Goals (xG) measures the quality of a scoring chance. It assigns a probability between 0.00 (impossible to score) and 1.00 (a guaranteed goal) to every attempt taken.
An xG value of 0.25 indicates that, based on historical shots taken under identical circumstances, an average professional scores that chance 25% of the time (or 1 in every 4 attempts).









Opportunity
Match Scenario
Historical Frequency
Expected Goals (xG)




Low-Threat Attempt
30-yard shot taken through defensive traffic
Converted in ~3% of attempts
0.03 xG


Medium-Threat Attempt
Header from an outswinging cross near the edge of the 18-yard box
Converted in ~12% of attempts
0.12 xG


High-Threat Attempt
Central penalty kick or uncontested back-post tap-in
Converted in ~78% of attempts
0.78 xG




What Factors Shape xG?

Distance to Goal: Closer attempts convert at significantly higher baseline rates.
Shooting Angle: Central attempts facing an open goal frame carry far more danger than tight-angle shots near the endline.
Striking Mechanism: Foot strikes convert at higher baseline rates than headers from the exact same pitch coordinates.
Phase of Play: Open-play counter-attacks against disorganized defenses yield higher probabilities than set-piece deliveries into crowded penalty boxes.







Key Takeaway: xG evaluates the chance creator. It answers: Did the team generate dangerous scoring positions, regardless of whether the final touch found the net?

title: Analytics Primer
section: 2. Expected Goals on Target (xGOT): Evaluating Shot Placement
text:
2. Expected Goals on Target (xGOT): Evaluating Shot Placement
While xG measures chance quality before the shot is taken, Expected Goals on Target (xGOT) - frequently called Post-Shot xG - evaluates the shot after it leaves the player’s boot or head.
Once a strike occurs, its trajectory, velocity, and landing destination inside the goal frame are known:









Phase
Metric Value
Event Detail
Practical Interpretation




Chance Opening
0.35 xG
Open look from 12 yards out
An above-average opportunity created by the attacking team.


Scenario A
0.00 xGOT
Attempt flies over crossbar or hits a blocking defender
Threat ends immediately; zero probability of beating the goalkeeper.


Scenario B
0.15 xGOT
Shot struck weakly toward the center of the goal frame
Poor placement reduces chance quality, making the save routine.


Scenario C
0.85 xGOT
Shot driven with pace into the upper side netting
Elite placement converts an average chance into a near-certain goal.









Key Takeaway: Comparing a player’s total xGOT to xG isolates finishing execution. Elite finishers consistently turn modest opportunities into difficult-to-save placements.

title: Analytics Primer
section: 3. The SAVE Profile: Advanced Goalkeeper Evaluation
text:
3. The SAVE Profile: Advanced Goalkeeper Evaluation
Evaluating a goalkeeper by raw goals conceded or clean sheets primarily reflects team defensive structure rather than individual goalkeeping skill. Even raw save percentage can be misleading: a keeper who faces 20 weak, rolling shots from 30 yards will post an artificially high save percentage, while a keeper who faces five uncontested point-blank breakaways will post a low save percentage despite making exceptional stops.
To isolate true shot-stopping skill, WoSo.Live evaluates goalkeepers across three core dimensions: Workload, Shot-Stopping Efficiency, and Game-to-Game Reliability.

Goals Prevented (GP)
The foundation of shot-stopping evaluation begins with Goals Prevented:

Goals Prevented = Total xGOT Faced − Goals Conceded


What it Means: If a goalkeeper faces 20.0 xGOT across a season and concedes only 15 goals, she has prevented +5.0 goals above what an average professional goalkeeper would have allowed facing those identical shots.
Positive Goals Prevented (+GP): The goalkeeper is outperforming expectation and rescuing her team through elite shot-stopping.
Negative Goals Prevented (−GP): The goalkeeper is allowing routine, savable attempts to enter the net.



Chance Quality (CQ) Tiers & Shot Diet
Every on-target attempt is classified into a Chance Quality (CQ) tier based on its Post-Shot Expected Goals (xGOT):










Danger Tier
xGOT Range
Opportunity Type
Pro Baseline Save Rate
Evaluation Focus




Low Danger (LD)
≤ 0.10 xGOT
Speculative long-distance strikes, weak headers, central rolling balls
~96% to 98%
Routine ball handling; allowing a goal here is a severe blunder.


Medium Danger (MD)
0.11 to 0.35 xGOT
Contested in-box strikes, angled drives, partially screened shots
~75% to 80%
Baseline professional competence; solid positioning and footwork prevail.


High Danger (HD)
> 0.35 xGOT
1v1 breakaways, point-blank rebounds, strikes into the upper-90 corners
~30% to 45%
Pure shot-stopping talent; where elite athleticism and reflex saves separate keepers.



The CQ Mix per 90 A goalkeeper’s workload is defined not only by the total shots she faces, but by the composition of those shots. A keeper with a high High-Danger Mix is under constant pressure from defensive breakdowns, while one with a heavy Low-Danger Mix is shielded by her backline.


Danger-Specific Save Rates (LDSv%, MDSv%, HDSv%)
Rather than evaluating goalkeepers on an aggregate save percentage, WoSo.Live measures save percentages within each individual danger tier against league and global benchmarks:

Low-Danger Save Percentage (LDSv%): The measure of baseline reliability. Elite goalkeepers rarely allow soft goals, maintaining an LDSv% above 98%.
Medium-Danger Save Percentage (MDSv%): Demonstrates consistency on standard in-box chances.
High-Danger Save Percentage (HDSv%): The separator for elite talent. Top-tier goalkeepers stop 40% to 50% of high-danger chances, whereas below-replacement keepers stop fewer than 25%.



Standardized Value & Consistency Metrics
To compare keepers playing behind airtight defenses with those playing behind leaky backlines, the SAVE dashboard introduces two standardized metrics:
Goals Prevented per 10 xGOT (GP/10xGOT) Raw Goals Prevented accumulates with playing time and shot volume. A keeper who faces 60 xGOT will naturally accumulate more raw Goals Prevented than a keeper who faces only 20 xGOT.

GP/10xGOT = (Total Goals Prevented / Total xGOT Faced) × 10


What it Means: For every 10 expected goals on target a keeper faces, how many did she prevent from crossing the line?
Baseline: A league-average goalkeeper sits at 0.00.
Elite Level: Ratings of +1.50 to +2.50 GP/10xGOT indicate a keeper who consistently stops 15% to 25% more goal threat than an average professional.

Above Expected Appearance Percentage (AxA%) Cumulative season totals can hide erratic form. A goalkeeper could compile +5.0 Goals Prevented on the season by posting a single miracle +6.0 performance, while playing below average in every other fixture.

AxA% = (Matches with Goals Prevented > 0 / Total Matches Played) × 100


What it Means: The percentage of appearances in which the goalkeeper outperformed expectation (GP > 0).
Baseline: Average professional goalkeepers post an AxA% between 45% and 50%.
Elite Consistency: Goalkeepers with an AxA% above 65% are game-to-game stabilizers who rarely cost their team points.



Bayesian Shot-Stopping Posteriors
Goalkeeping sample sizes are notoriously volatile. If a backup saves the first four shots she faces in her debut, her raw save rate is 100%, but she is not necessarily the best keeper in the league.
WoSo.Live uses Conjugate Empirical Bayes modeling to estimate a goalkeeper’s true talent distribution:

The Baseline Prior: Every keeper begins anchored to the global professional baseline (a bell curve centered at 0.00 Goals Prevented per shot).
Live Posterior Updating: Each time a shot is faced, the model updates the curve based on the shot’s difficulty (xGOT) and the actual outcome (goal or save).
Curve Center (Peak): Represents the keeper’s most likely true shot-stopping talent. Shifted right = elite shot-stopper; shifted left = below average.
Curve Width (Spread): Represents statistical certainty. A wide, flat curve indicates high uncertainty (small sample size). As a goalkeeper faces 100, 200, and 300 shots, the curve narrows into a tall, sharp peak, confirming her established talent level.

Head-to-Head Probability of Superiority When comparing two goalkeepers, single-number averages ignore sample confidence. The Head-to-Head engine calculates the exact mathematical overlap of both full posterior curves:

Probability of Superiority = P(Talent of Keeper A > Talent of Keeper B)

This answers the scouting question directly: Accounting for sample size, shot difficulty, and historical variance, what is the exact probability that Goalkeeper A is genuinely a better shot-stopper than Goalkeeper B?

title: Analytics Primer
section: 4. Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus (RAPM): Complete On-Pitch Impact
text:
4. Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus (RAPM): Complete On-Pitch Impact
Most decisive soccer contributions occur off the ball: opening passing lanes with an uncredited decoy run, applying a pressing angle that forces a hurried turnover, or tracking a runner to prevent a cutback cross. Traditional box-score tallies miss these events entirely.
Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus (RAPM) isolates a player’s direct impact on her team’s goal differential per 90 minutes.

The Modeling Sequence

Stint-by-Stint Segmentation: Matches are divided into distinct stints whenever a substitution, goal, or red card alters on-pitch personnel or game state.
Single-Stage Environmental Conditioning: The model solves for player talent and environmental context simultaneously within a unified design matrix. Rather than residualizing through an initial unregularized stage (which risks over-attributing superstar talent to match context), structural environmental factors enter with a penalty factor of zero (\(\lambda_{env} = 0\)), guaranteeing unpenalized estimation of baseline conditions:

Venue Advantage: Empirical Bayes regularized home advantage bounded in \([+0.0300, +0.2490]\).
Score Differential: State clamped strictly within \([-4.0, +4.0]\) to prevent garbage-time distortions.
Rest Dynamics: Continuous cubic natural splines \(ns(df = 3)\) on rest days, coalesced to a 7.0-day default.
Flight & Minute Load: Continuous splines capturing acute travel mileage and accumulated fatigue.

Player & Position-Specific Ridge Shrinkage: RAPM applies L2 Ridge regularization to isolate individual contributions independent of teammates and opponents. Regularization multipliers are structurally partitioned:

Outfielders: Standard baseline regularization (\(c_{outfield} = 1.0\)).
Goalkeepers: Regularization multiplier \(c_{gk} \in [2.5, 7.5]\) tuned via 10-fold cross-validation to account for post-shot variance.
Managers: Coach baseline multiplier \(c_{coach} \in [1.0, 20.0]\) isolating tactical system effects.




Reading RAPM Values

Offensive RAPM (xGF/90): Expected goals her team generates per 90 minutes driven by her presence on the pitch.
Defensive RAPM (xGA/90): Expected goals her team suppresses per 90 minutes. Positive numbers indicate stronger defensive suppression.
Net RAPM/90: Total isolated possession value (Offensive RAPM + Defensive RAPM). A rating of +0.25 means a player improves her team’s net goal differential by a quarter-goal every full match.

title: Analytics Primer
section: 5. Spatial RAPM: Mapping Where Threat Occurs
text:
5. Spatial RAPM: Mapping Where Threat Occurs
While Net RAPM produces a single overall score, Spatial RAPM illustrates where on the pitch a player makes her impact.
WoSo.Live partitions the attacking half into 91 distinct zones (a Deep Zone plus a 90-hexagon grid in the final third). The model solves for a player’s isolated offensive creation and defensive suppression inside each individual zone.
These spatial vectors are smoothed using thin-plate splines and rendered via Tanaka shaded elevation contours:

Red and Orange Elevation Ridges: High-impact zones where a player generates significant offensive threat or concedes more threat than league average when the player is on the pitch.
Blue Depressions: Zones where the team produces less threat or delivers heavy defensive suppression.
Contour Peaks: Lighted from the upper-left to visually display the depth and sharpness of a player’s local territorial influence.

title: Analytics Primer
section: 6. Wins Above Replacement (WAR): Converting Talent into Standings Value
text:
6. Wins Above Replacement (WAR): Converting Talent into Standings Value
A rate metric like Net RAPM/90 measures per-minute efficiency, but it does not account for availability. A substitute who plays 150 elite minutes off the bench provides less aggregate value to a club over a season than a reliable starter logging 2,500 minutes at an above-average level.
The Wins Above Replacement (WAR) framework connects per-minute performance with playing time to evaluate a player’s total contribution to her team’s standings position.

The Valuation Chain









Step
Metric
Mathematical Formula
Practical Meaning




1. Per-Minute Talent
Net RAPM / 90
Single-Stage Ridge Regression
Isolated player rate impact per 90 minutes.


2. Average Baseline
Goals Above Average (GAA)
(Net xG per 90 × Nineties) + Finishing Talent
Net goals produced relative to an average player over the same minutes.


3. Replacement Baseline
Goals Above Replacement (GAR)
GAA − (Replacement Floor × Nineties)
Net goals produced relative to an accessible bench or reserve replacement.


4. Standings Impact
Points Above Replacement (PAR)
GAR × 0.65
League table standings points delivered to the team.


5. Match Victories
Wins Above Replacement (WAR)
GAR / 3.65
Total match victories directly added by the player.


6. Season Efficiency
Paced WAR (WAR/30)
(WAR / Nineties) × 30
Value paced to a full 30-match season (minimum 450 minutes).





Core Valuation Concepts

The “Replacement Level” Benchmark
Average talent (GAA = 0.0) is not the baseline of value. If a starting central defender suffers an injury, her club cannot sign a league-average starter mid-season; they must rely on a replacement player - a reserve from the back end of the squad or a youth call-up.

Outfield Replacement Floors: Defined by the bottom 15th percentile of active rotation players in each position group (Center Back, Fullback, Midfielder, Forward), bounded between −0.25 and −0.12 goals per 90 minutes.
Goalkeeper Replacement Floor: Anchored to −0.104 goals per 90 minutes to prevent small backup samples from distorting starter ratings.



Goals to Points (PAR) and Wins (WAR)

Points Above Replacement (PAR): In professional soccer, each +1.0 in net goal differential historically yields approximately 0.65 standings points (PAR = GAR × 0.65).
Wins Above Replacement (WAR): It takes approximately 3.65 net goals above replacement to produce one additional team victory (WAR = GAR / 3.65).









WAR Range
Production Tier
Typical Profile




+3.0 to +4.5 WAR
MVP Contender
Dominant league leader responsible for 3 to 4 team victories over replacement.


+1.5 to +2.5 WAR
High-End Starter
All-League caliber player who consistently swings matches.


+0.8 to +1.4 WAR
Solid Starter
Dependable everyday starter playing above replacement level.


0.0 to +0.5 WAR
Rotational Depth
Bench contributor providing replacement-level support.


< 0.0 WAR
Below Replacement
Player performing below readily available reserve options.





Paced WAR (WAR/30)
Because injuries or transfers limit total minutes, Paced WAR (WAR/30) standardizes performance to a full 30-match season (2,700 minutes) to display per-game efficiency.
To prevent small-sample cameos from distorting the leaderboard, Paced WAR enforces a strict 450-minute qualification floor (five full matches). Players below 450 minutes receive an NA rating, preventing a player who logged 20 fortunate minutes from displaying an unearned 7.0 WAR pace.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
text:
← All Articles



By Ian Fleming · November 24, 2026
Recently, Christopher Gerrish at American Soccer Analysis published a thoughtful look at the defense problem in soccer, asking why Wins Above Replacement (WAR) still struggles to measure defending cleanly.
Anyone who works with soccer data runs into that wall eventually. On the attacking side, we have comfortable tools to track who creates chances (xG) and who takes dangerous shots. Defending is trickier, mostly because box-score stats tend to measure how busy a defender was rather than whether she actually helped prevent goals.
Since WoSo.Live takes a slightly different modeling path than ASA, using adjusted plus-minus for outfield players and shot-level models for goalkeepers, Gerrish’s piece made us wonder how well our own numbers hold up under similar tests. To find out, we checked our models across 21 women’s professional leagues, covering more than 500 team-seasons, over 2,300 matches, and 123,146 shots on target faced by over 2,100 goalkeepers. Wherever possible, we trained ratings strictly on Season 1 and graded them only on Season 2 games they had never seen.
Here is what held up, what surprised us, and what we tuned afterward.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
text:
The Tackle Trap Holds Everywhere
Picture two center backs. One plays on a deep-lying underdog and piles up clearances, blocks, and tackles every match. Another plays for a high-possession favorite whose best defending happens when she shuts down a counterattack before the pass is ever played.
Gerrish showed that interrupting events had almost no link to future goals conceded in the NWSL. Across 21 leagues, we saw the same pattern. Defensive counting stats (tackles, interceptions, clearances, blocks, and recoveries) repeat surprisingly well from year to year (0.82 overall, and even 0.80 when a player switches clubs). The catch is what they measure. Inside a season, teams with busier defenders concede more expected goals, not fewer. Looking ahead to next season, prior tackle and clearance volume predicts essentially zero percent of goals allowed (r = -0.01). Counting stats tell us plenty about a player’s workload, just very little about defensive quality.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
section: How Plus-Minus Sees the Off-Ball Game
text:
How Plus-Minus Sees the Off-Ball Game
At the risk of oversimplification, WoSo.Live rates outfielders the way basketball and hockey analysts evaluate skaters: by tracking what happens to expected goal differential whenever a player is on the pitch. Every match splits into segments whenever a sub, goal, or red card happens. The model adjusts for teammates, opponents, home advantage, score state, rest, and travel, then pulls smaller samples back toward league average.
So what do we actually see? Inside the same season, player and coach ratings explain roughly 76% of team points-per-game differences across 21 leagues, very close to ASA’s numbers. When we predict Season 2 strictly from Season 1 ratings without peeking ahead, that figure drops to 51%. That gap is a useful reminder that same-season tests soak up a lot of shared team rhythm. Even so, explaining half of next season’s standings variance from prior data is genuine signal, and defensive RAPM pulls real weight on its own (r = -0.58 vs. next year’s goals conceded; r = -0.60 vs. expected goals allowed). Across more than 2,300 unseen matches, adding defense on top of offense gave our match model its largest boost in accuracy.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
section: The Mover Test: Does Defense Travel?
text:
The Mover Test: Does Defense Travel?
The hardest question in any plus-minus model is context. Did a defender earn her rating on her own, or alongside great teammates and a sharp coach? To test this, we looked at players with at least 450 minutes in back-to-back seasons in the same league and split them into 1,655 Stayers (same club) and 464 Movers (new club).










Player Group (Same League, Year-over-Year)

Both halves of that table matter. First, roughly two-thirds of a player’s year-over-year stability fades when she changes jerseys (0.54 down to 0.19). Teammates and systems explain a lot, and no metric completely separates a defender from her backline. Yet both offense (0.17) and defense (0.12) remain clearly positive in new locker rooms under new managers. Individual defense is noisier than offense, though a real piece of it travels. (This pass covered intra-league moves; testing cross-league transfers is next on our list.)

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
section: How Does Defensive RAPM Compare to ASA’s Approach?
text:
How Does Defensive RAPM Compare to ASA’s Approach?
It is fair to ask how WoSo.Live’s defensive RAPM stacks up against the tracking-based metrics ASA proposed, such as prevented transition shots and off-ball positioning. In the NWSL, defensive RAPM explains roughly 76% of team goals allowed within the same season, compared with about 48% for ASA’s composite tracking defense. That gap needs a grain of salt, though, because plus-minus is fitted directly to expected goals allowed in those games, giving it a natural advantage on same-season checks.
Where defensive RAPM holds a clear edge right now is proven out-of-sample reach. ASA only had two non-consecutive seasons of tracking data (2018 and 2023), so it could not yet test year-to-year predictions or player movement. By contrast, defensive RAPM holds up across 21 leagues and over 2,300 unseen future matches, without needing optical tracking cameras.
At the same time, ASA’s bottom-up positioning work tackles the exact spot where plus-minus is weakest: individual credit assignment. As the Mover Test shows, teammates and systems carry heavy weight in RAPM. Tracking whether a defender stays goal-side or closes a passing lane is much steadier player to player (0.68 to 0.87 split-half consistency) and helps show who actually stopped the play. Rather than competing, the two views come at defense from opposite ends (outcomes versus process), and as tracking data spreads, those off-ball habits could eventually make plus-minus priors even sharper.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
section: Goalkeepers Really Are on an Island
text:
Goalkeepers Really Are on an Island
Once you account for the outfielders in front of her, a goalkeeper’s on-off defensive plus-minus shows almost no tie to shot-stopping (r = 0.10) and adds nothing when predicting future goals allowed.
Measuring keepers directly on post-shot expected goals (xGOT, based on shot difficulty once the ball is struck on frame) across 123,146 shots tells a much cleaner story. First, pulling small samples back toward a global average keeps short-term hot streaks from going haywire while letting true skill separate once a keeper faces 75 to 150 shots. Second, unlike outfielders, returning keepers with 20 or more shots kept every bit of their consistency after changing clubs: 0.24 year-over-year for movers versus 0.23 for stayers (and 0.31 among regular starters facing 40+ shots). We also checked whether shot-stopping splits into “highlight saves” versus routine stops, and found one unified skill curve works better.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
text:
The Sweeper-Keeper Question
Ann-Katrin Berger winning the 2026 NWSL Goalkeeper of the Year award brought a long-simmering debate back to the surface. Should an award value a keeper’s sweeping and distribution alongside her shot-stopping, or focus mainly on keeping shots out of the net? In the 2026 regular season, Berger was a strong shot-stopper for Gotham FC (+4.86 goals prevented on 27.86 xGOT faced, or +1.74 per 10 xGOT, placing 4th in our Bayesian ratings) while putting up eye-catching numbers outside her box: 1.63 sweeper actions per 90 minutes, nearly four times the 0.41 league average, alongside a league-best 1.22 high claims per 90 plus 34.6 accurate passes per 90. Yet other starters put together bigger shot-stopping seasons under much heavier fire, led by Jane Campbell (+13.79 goals prevented on 55.79 xGOT faced, or +2.47 per 10 xGOT), Jordan Silkowitz (+8.07), and Katie Lund (+7.51 in 15 starts).
To see how those two sides of goalkeeping fit together, we ran the same tests across our 21-league database and the four leagues with full sweeper tracking (NWSL, WSL, France, and Australia). First, sweeper and ball-playing stats sit almost completely separate from shot-stopping (r = 0.01 for sweeper actions) and add nothing positive to goalkeeper plus-minus. In fact, busy defensive actions like clearances and recoveries fall into the exact same workload trap as outfield tackles because underdogs face more pressure.
They are also tightly tied to club tactics. Across all 21 leagues, keeper passing volume drops from 0.70 year-over-year consistency for stayers to 0.35 when a keeper switches clubs, while two completely different keepers playing for the same club still correlate at 0.36 (and between 0.31 and 0.49 across sweeper, touch, and passing metrics in the four tracking-detail leagues). Pure shot-stopping does the exact opposite: 0.01 between different keepers at the same club, and 0.30 when a keeper changes teams. And when we predict next season’s team results across 275 clubs while controlling for outfield RAPM and prior team baselines, shot-stopping is the only goalkeeper trait that reliably moves future goals conceded and points per game. Sweeping, passing, claiming, and clearing counts add no consistent out-of-sample lift to future goals, expected goals, or points.
Just like ASA’s point on outfield tackles, those null findings do not prove ball-playing or aggressive sweeping has zero worth. Counting how often a keeper clears a through ball or completes a short pass cannot capture pass difficulty under pressure or the breakaway that never materialized because a keeper stepped off her line early. What the numbers do show is that, with the event data we have today, shot-stopping is the one goalkeeper skill we can cleanly untangle from team style and link to future standings. Awards like Berger’s sit right on that boundary between what stands out clearly on film and what our models can currently prove.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
section: Where Do We Go From Here?
text:
Where Do We Go From Here?
The real value of checking your own work is spotting quiet flaws you can fix. This review led to three practical updates in WoSo.Live:

Anchoring small-league keepers globally: Estimating spread inside smaller 30-keeper leagues created bouncy ratings from year to year. Tying every league to our 123,000-shot global baseline keeps smaller leagues steady without flattening standout seasons.
Giving unseen signings a club starting point: Player-based models beat simple team ratings in the balanced NWSL, yet assuming unseen signings are exact 0.00 league average pulled powerhouse clubs down in high-turnover European leagues. Adding a light club-strength prior for new signings, scaled by how much talent clusters by club in each league, improved forecasts across the board.
Adjusting goal-to-win math for league parity: In the tight NWSL, an extra goal per match adds about 0.66 points per game. In top-heavy leagues where contenders win 3-0 or 4-0 regularly, marginal goals run into diminishing returns (0.48 overall in lopsided leagues, and 0.36 in Scotland’s SWPL 1). Accounting for team disparity cut our points-per-goal conversion error nearly fourfold.

title: Out of Sample, Out of Position: Testing Soccer Defense and Goalkeeping
section: So What Can We Take Away From This?
text:
So What Can We Take Away From This?
Soccer defense will probably never boil down to one spotless stat, and patience still goes a long way when judging players over a single season. Too much happens through shared movement across eleven players.
Still, once we move past counting busy actions and judge models strictly against future games, the signal is real. Adjusted plus-minus captures genuine, portable defending, post-shot Bayesian models isolate goalkeeping skill, and both add real predictive value. The picture isn’t perfect yet, and it doesn’t have to be to help us see the game a little more clearly.

text: WoSo.Live hosts a suite of advanced quantitative tools and interactive applications dedicated to women’s soccer analytics. Featuring custom Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus (RAPM) modeling, expected goals (xG) shot simulations, and comprehensive tournament forecasting, the platform aims to bridge the gap between complex data science and accessible visual insights for the global women’s game.
